meta.description: Self-taught backend developer (TypeScript, Node.js) focused on real-time systems, currently in a BTS SIO (SLAM) program. Projects, experience, and tech watch.

about.paragraph: I’ve been coding for over seven years now: Scratch in primary school to start, then more seriously self-taught, mostly in TypeScript and Node.js, with a soft spot for real-time systems. Now in my second year of BTS SIO (SLAM). Most of the projects below grew out of that interest rather than an actual need.

descriptions.odm: Real-time network monitoring for an industrial site: interactive map, ICMP ping diagnostics, live SSE feed.
descriptions.aurum: Terminal trading panel for gold (XAUUSD), orders executed live via the cTrader MCP, market structure computed locally.
descriptions.zen: Multi-purpose Discord bot: moderation, utilities, commands loaded dynamically by category.
descriptions.borning: Web platform for Alstom’s internal multi-sport challenge, built during an internship in Charleroi.

descriptions.mairie: Town hall IT internship: hardware maintenance, network administration, first-line technical support.
descriptions.nyxo: An open-source TypeScript package for building Discord bots, built to cover the API in depth rather than paper over it. Discontinued now, but it’s what I actually learned backend development on, over more than two years.
descriptions.freelance: Full-stack websites for clients, as an independent freelancer.
descriptions.alstom: At Alstom: rebuilt the ODM Monitoring Alstom network monitoring tool (see Projects), then moved into technical-assistant duties: workstation replacements and hardware support.

meta.title: Post-quantum cryptography · Tech watch · Tom B.
meta.description: A tech watch on post-quantum cryptography: NIST’s FIPS 203/204/205 standards, the migration timeline, and real-world adoption in 2026.

veille.title: Post-quantum cryptography
intro: In August 2024, NIST turned a decade of theoretical research into concrete federal standards: FIPS 203, 204, and 205. What used to be an academic conference topic became, overnight, a compliance obligation for anyone protecting long-lived data.

The stakes fit in one phrase: “harvest now, decrypt later.” Traffic encrypted today with classical algorithms (RSA, ECC) can be intercepted and stored as-is, waiting for a sufficiently powerful quantum computer to decrypt it retroactively. Migrating before that day isn’t optional: it’s a race against a threat with no confirmed deadline.

descriptions.mlkem: Establishes a shared secret between two parties, the post-quantum equivalent of Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Lattice-based, and the fastest of the three, which is why it’s already the one deployed in TLS and encrypted messaging.
descriptions.mldsa: A digital signature scheme derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium, also lattice-based. Larger signatures than RSA (up to 4.6 KB), but the default candidate for document and certificate authentication.
descriptions.slhdsa: A hash-based signature scheme rather than a lattice-based one: a deliberately different mathematical assumption, kept as a safety net in case lattices ever turn out to be breakable. Slower and heavier (up to 50 KB), reserved for cases where caution outweighs performance.

descriptions.y2016: NIST launches its international post-quantum standardization competition.
descriptions.y2022: Kyber, Dilithium, SPHINCS+, and Falcon are selected as finalists.
descriptions.y2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) are published as final standards.
descriptions.y2025: HQC is selected as a fifth algorithm: a second key-exchange mechanism based on error-correcting codes rather than lattices, so the standard doesn’t rest on one mathematical family alone.
descriptions.y2027: NSA deadline (CNSA 2.0): every new U.S. government system must support post-quantum cryptography.
descriptions.y2035: Target for full quantum resistance across all U.S. National Security Systems.

adoption.heading: Real-world adoption
adoption.paragraph: Chrome, Edge, and Firefox now enable a hybrid key exchange by default (X25519MLKEM768, combining the old and new standards); Signal and iMessage have already switched their protocols over. At Cloudflare, the share of TLS traffic encrypted with post-quantum key exchange went from roughly 2% in early 2024 to over 67% by April 2026, one of the fastest cryptographic migrations ever measured. The gap sits on the enterprise side: most are testing, few have shipped it to production.
